claim: During embryonic development, the mesoderm undergoes patterning into diverse lineages including axial, paraxial, and lateral plate mesoderm (LPM).
source: During embryonic development, the mesoderm undergoes patterning into diverse lineages including axial, paraxial, and lateral plate mesoderm (LPM).
evidence: This is a statement about established developmental biology knowledge presented in the abstract.

claim: Within the LPM, the intermediate mesoderm (IM) forms kidney and urogenital tract progenitor cells.
source: Within the LPM, the so-called intermediate mesoderm (IM) forms kidney and urogenital tract progenitor cells, while the remaining LPM forms cardiovascular, hematopoietic, mesothelial, and additional progenitor cells.
evidence: This statement draws from established developmental biology knowledge about mesoderm patterning.

claim: The remaining LPM forms cardiovascular, hematopoietic, mesothelial, and additional progenitor cells.
source: Within the LPM, the so-called intermediate mesoderm (IM) forms kidney and urogenital tract progenitor cells, while the remaining LPM forms cardiovascular, hematopoietic, mesothelial, and additional progenitor cells.
evidence: This statement draws from established developmental biology knowledge about mesoderm patterning.

claim: CEP83 is a centriolar component necessary for primary cilia formation.
source: Here, we found that the centrosomal protein 83 (CEP83), a centriolar component necessary for primary cilia formation and mutated in pediatric kidney disease, influences the differentiation of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) toward IM.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and established knowledge about CEP83 function.

claim: CEP83 is mutated in pediatric kidney disease.
source: Here, we found that the centrosomal protein 83 (CEP83), a centriolar component necessary for primary cilia formation and mutated in pediatric kidney disease, influences the differentiation of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) toward IM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Failler et al., 2014 in the introduction.

claim: CEP83 influences the differentiation of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) toward intermediate mesoderm.
source: Here, we found that the centrosomal protein 83 (CEP83), a centriolar component necessary for primary cilia formation and mutated in pediatric kidney disease, influences the differentiation of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) toward IM.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: hiPSCs with homozygous CEP83 inactivation were normal regarding morphology and transcriptome.
source: While hiPSCs with homozygous CEP83 inactivation were normal regarding morphology and transcriptome, their induced differentiation into IM progenitor cells was perturbed.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements showing morphology and RNA-seq data.

claim: Mesodermal cells induced after 7 days of monolayer culture of CEP83-deficient hiPSCs exhibited absent or elongated primary cilia.
source: Mesodermal cells induced after 7 days of monolayer culture of CEP83-deficient hiPCS exhibited absent or elongated primary cilia, displayed decreased expression of critical IM genes (PAX8, EYA1, HOXB7), and an aberrant induction of LPM markers (e.g. FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2D-G showing ciliary abnormalities.

claim: CEP83-deficient cells at day 7 displayed decreased expression of critical IM genes (PAX8, EYA1, HOXB7).
source: Mesodermal cells induced after 7 days of monolayer culture of CEP83-deficient hiPCS exhibited absent or elongated primary cilia, displayed decreased expression of critical IM genes (PAX8, EYA1, HOXB7), and an aberrant induction of LPM markers (e.g. FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: CEP83-deficient cells at day 7 showed aberrant induction of LPM markers (e.g. FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2).
source: Mesodermal cells induced after 7 days of monolayer culture of CEP83-deficient hiPCS exhibited absent or elongated primary cilia, displayed decreased expression of critical IM genes (PAX8, EYA1, HOXB7), and an aberrant induction of LPM markers (e.g. FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Wildtype cells differentiated to form kidney tubules and glomerular-like structures upon organoid culture.
source: Upon subsequent organoid culture, wildtype cells differentiated to form kidney tubules and glomerular-like structures, whereas CEP83-deficient cells failed to generate kidney cell types, instead upregulating cardiomyocyte, vascular, and more general LPM progenitor markers.
evidence: This is supported by histology and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3.

claim: CEP83-deficient cells failed to generate kidney cell types upon organoid culture.
source: Upon subsequent organoid culture, wildtype cells differentiated to form kidney tubules and glomerular-like structures, whereas CEP83-deficient cells failed to generate kidney cell types, instead upregulating cardiomyocyte, vascular, and more general LPM progenitor markers.
evidence: This is supported by histology and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3 showing absence of kidney markers.

claim: CEP83-deficient organoids upregulated cardiomyocyte, vascular, and more general LPM progenitor markers.
source: Upon subsequent organoid culture, wildtype cells differentiated to form kidney tubules and glomerular-like structures, whereas CEP83-deficient cells failed to generate kidney cell types, instead upregulating cardiomyocyte, vascular, and more general LPM progenitor markers.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 7 showing upregulation of ISL1, TBX1, SOX7, SOX11, etc.

claim: CEP83 regulates the balance of IM and LPM formation from human pluripotent stem cells.
source: Our data suggest that CEP83 regulates the balance of IM and LPM formation from human pluripotent stem cells, identifying a potential link between centriolar or ciliary function and mesodermal lineage induction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing altered IM/LPM marker expression.

claim: CEP83 is a component of distal appendages (DAPs) of centrioles.
source: The centrosomal protein 83 (CEP83) is a component of distal appendages (DAPs) of centrioles.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Lo et al., 2019; Tanos et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018; Kurtulmus et al., 2018; Wheway et al., 2015; Bowler et al., 2019; Failler et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2020; Mansour et al., 2021).

claim: DAPs are involved in the anchoring of the mother centriole to the cell membrane.
source: DAPs are involved in the anchoring of the mother centriole to the cell membrane, an early and critical step in ciliogenesis (Lo et al., 2019; Tanos et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018; Kurtulmus et al., 2018; Wheway et al., 2015; Bowler et al., 2019; Failler et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2020; Mansour et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about DAP function.

claim: CEP83 recruits other DAP components to the ciliary base.
source: CEP83 recruits other DAP components to the ciliary base, and loss of CEP83 disrupts ciliogenesis (Tanos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of CEP83 disrupts ciliogenesis.
source: CEP83 recruits other DAP components to the ciliary base, and loss of CEP83 disrupts ciliogenesis (Tanos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013 and experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Removal of CEP83 in radial glial progenitors disrupts DAP assembly and impairs the anchoring of the centrosome to the apical membrane.
source: In radial glial progenitors, removal of CEP83 disrupts DAP assembly and impairs the anchoring of the centrosome to the apical membrane as well as primary ciliogenesis (Yang et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2018 and Shao et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations of CEP83 in humans have been associated with infantile nephronophthisis.
source: Mutations of CEP83 in humans have been associated with infantile nephronophthisis (Failler et al., 2014), an early onset kidney disease that results in end-stage renal disease before the age of 3 years (Hildebrandt, 2004; Luo and Tao, 2018) and additional organ anomalies (Failler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Failler et al., 2014.

claim: Infantile nephronophthisis is an early onset kidney disease that results in end-stage renal disease before the age of 3 years.
source: Mutations of CEP83 in humans have been associated with infantile nephronophthisis (Failler et al., 2014), an early onset kidney disease that results in end-stage renal disease before the age of 3 years (Hildebrandt, 2004; Luo and Tao, 2018) and additional organ anomalies (Failler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hildebrandt, 2004 and Luo and Tao, 2018.

claim: Three hiPSCs clones designated CEP83−/− (KO1, KO2, and KO3) carried deletions within CEP83 exon 7.
source: Three hiPSCs clones designated CEP83−/− (KO1, KO2, and KO3) carried deletions within CEP83 exon 7, each of which led to an induction of a premature stop codon resulting in a predicted truncated protein (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The deletions in CEP83 exon 7 led to induction of a premature stop codon resulting in a predicted truncated protein.
source: Three hiPSCs clones designated CEP83−/− (KO1, KO2, and KO3) carried deletions within CEP83 exon 7, each of which led to an induction of a premature stop codon resulting in a predicted truncated protein (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CEP83 knockout clones exhibited a complete loss of CEP83 protein by immunoblotting.
source: These clones exhibited a complete loss of CEP83 protein by immunoblotting (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: All six clones (WT and KO) were morphologically indistinguishable by brightfield microscopy.
source: All six clones were morphologically indistinguishable (by brightfield microscopy) and had similar overall gene expression profiles (by bulk RNA-seq and qRT-PCR), including pluripotency and lineage marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by brightfield images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: WT and KO clones had similar overall gene expression profiles including pluripotency and lineage marker expression.
source: All six clones were morphologically indistinguishable (by brightfield microscopy) and had similar overall gene expression profiles (by bulk RNA-seq and qRT-PCR), including pluripotency and lineage marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq heatmap in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphism analysis confirmed identical karyotypes of all six clones.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphism - analysis confirmed identical karyotypes of all six clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by karyotype analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: After 7 days of culture, WT and KO cells exhibited an indistinguishable morphology by bright field microscopy.
source: After 7 days of culture (D7), WT and KO cells exhibited an indistinguishable morphology by bright field microscopy (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by brightfield images in Figure 2B and C.

claim: CEP83-deficient cells at day 7 exhibited abnormal primary cilia formation.
source: Immunostaining for acetylated tubulin, however, indicated abnormal primary cilia formation in CEP83-deficient cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The number of ciliated cells was reduced from approximately 30% in WT clones to less than 10% in KO clones at day 7.
source: The number of ciliated cells was reduced from approximately 30% (in WT clones) to less than 10% (in KO clones) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Among ciliated cells at day 7, the length of cilia was increased from 2 to 5 µm in WT clones to 5–13 µm in KO clones.
source: Among ciliated cells, the length of cilia was increased from 2 to 5 µm (in WT clones) to 5–13 µm (in KO clones) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Organoids harvested from WT clones after 25 days of culture had formed patterned kidney epithelial-like structures.
source: Organoids harvested from WT clones after a total of 25 days of culture (D25) had formed patterned kidney epithelial-like structures, including NPHS1-positive glomerulus-like structures, Lotus tetragonolobus lectin-positive proximal tubule-like, and E-cadherin (CDH1)-positive distal tubule-like structures (Figure 3A, C and E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histology and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A, C, E.

claim: CEP83−/− organoids at day 25 were composed of monomorphic cells with a mesenchyme-like appearance.
source: In contrast, CEP83−/− organoids at day 25 were composed of monomorphic cells with a mesenchyme-like appearance, which stained negative for an array of kidney cell markers (Figure 3B, D and F).
evidence: This is supported by histology and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B, D, F.

claim: Kidney epithelial-like structures formed only in WT but not in CEP83−/− organoids.
source: Kidney epithelial-like structures formed only in WT but not in CEP83−/− organoids (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: Primary cilia were found in fewer cells of CEP83−/− organoids (<5% of cells) and were abnormally elongated.
source: Similar to the findings in day 7 cells reported above, primary cilia were found in fewer cells of CEP83−/− organoids (<5% of cells) and were abnormally elongated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several genes associated with kidney development and kidney epithelial differentiation were differentially expressed with high expression in WT organoids but low or absent expression in CEP83−/− organoids.
source: Several genes associated with kidney development and kidney epithelial differentiation were differentially expressed with high expression in WT organoids but showed comparatively low or absent expression in CEP83−/− organoids: these genes included kidney-specific lineage genes (PAX2, PAX8), and lineage/differentiation markers of glomerular cells (NPHS1, PODXL, WT1, PTPRO), proximal (HNF1B, LRP2, CUBN), and distal (EMX2, MAL2, EPCAM, GATA3) kidney epithelial cells (Figure 3H–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3H-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A marked upregulation of nephron progenitor marker genes (GATA3, HOXB7, HOXD11, EYA1) was observed in both WT and CEP83−/− cells at day 7.
source: A marked upregulation of nephron progenitor marker genes (GATA3, HOXB7, HOXD11, EYA1) (Bilous et al., 1992; Grote et al., 2006; Kress et al., 1990; Srinivas et al., 1999; Wellik et al., 2002; Mugford et al., 2008a; Ruf et al., 2004; Sajithlal et al., 2005) was observed in both WT and CEP83−/− cells at day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the differentiation path of pluripotent CEP83−/− cells to IM nephron progenitors was largely intact.
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The differentiation path of pluripotent CEP83−/− cells to IM nephron progenitors was largely intact.
source: A marked upregulation of nephron progenitor marker genes (GATA3, HOXB7, HOXD11, EYA1) (Bilous et al., 1992; Grote et al., 2006; Kress et al., 1990; Srinivas et al., 1999; Wellik et al., 2002; Mugford et al., 2008a; Ruf et al., 2004; Sajithlal et al., 2005) was observed in both WT and CEP83−/− cells at day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the differentiation path of pluripotent CEP83−/− cells to IM nephron progenitors was largely intact.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nephron progenitor markers are upregulated in both WT and KO cells.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing obtained transcriptomes from 27,328 cells representing WT1, WT2, KO1, and KO2 clones.
source: We obtained transcriptomes from 27,328 cells, representing clones WT1 (experiment 1: 3768 cells), WT2 (experiment 2: 5793 cells), KO1 (experiment 1: 8503 cells), and KO2 (experiment 2: 9264 cells).
evidence: This describes the experimental data obtained from single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: The first principal component (dimension 1, explaining 54% of expression variation) was driven by the genotype (WT vs. KO).
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) using pseudo-bulk expression data of the top 1000 highly variable genes (HVGs) indicated that the first principal component (dimension 1, explaining 54% of expression variation) was driven by the genotype (WT vs. KO), while the second principal component (dimension 2, explaining 51% of expression variation) was driven by a batch effect of the two experiments (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The second principal component (dimension 2, explaining 51% of expression variation) was driven by a batch effect of the two experiments.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) using pseudo-bulk expression data of the top 1000 highly variable genes (HVGs) indicated that the first principal component (dimension 1, explaining 54% of expression variation) was driven by the genotype (WT vs. KO), while the second principal component (dimension 2, explaining 51% of expression variation) was driven by a batch effect of the two experiments (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Unbiased clustering of single-cell data resulted in 10 different cell states/clusters (0–9).
source: We combined all cells and generated a uniform manifold approximation and projection plot uncovering 10 different cell states/clusters (0–9; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by UMAP plot in Figure 4B.

claim: Clusters 1, 3, and 4 represented kidney progenitors/nascent nephrons in different phases of the cell cycle.
source: We identified marker genes for each cluster (Figure 4C), indicating that clusters 1, 3, and 4 represented kidney progenitors/nascent nephrons (expressing, e.g., PAX8, EYA1, HOXB7) in different phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is supported by marker gene analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cluster 5 represented damaged cells expressing high levels of mitochondrial RNAs.
source: However, one cluster representing damaged cells (cluster 5) was observed at numerically higher percentages in KO cells compared to WT cells. Cluster 5 cells expressed high levels of mitochondrial RNAs, and staining for active caspase 3 demonstrated an increased percentage of apoptotic cells in KO samples compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial RNA analysis and caspase 3 staining in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cluster 5 was observed at numerically higher percentages in KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: However, one cluster representing damaged cells (cluster 5) was observed at numerically higher percentages in KO cells compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by cluster proportion analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Staining for active caspase 3 demonstrated an increased percentage of apoptotic cells in KO samples compared to controls.
source: Cluster 5 cells expressed high levels of mitochondrial RNAs, and staining for active caspase 3 demonstrated an increased percentage of apoptotic cells in KO samples compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by caspase 3 immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-F.

claim: A numerically lower percentage of KO cells (11.9 and 12.5% in KO clones) contributed to cluster 1 when compared with WT cells (25.9 and 36.3% in WT clones).
source: We focused on kidney progenitors (clusters 1, 3, and 4) and found that a numerically lower percentage of KO cells (11.9 and 12.5% in KO clones) contributed to cluster 1 when compared with WT cells (25.9 and 36.3% in WT clones) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cluster proportion analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Similar percentages of WT and KO cells were represented in kidney progenitor clusters 3 and 4.
source: In contrast, similar percentages of WT and KO cells were represented in kidney progenitor clusters 3 and 4 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by cluster proportion analysis in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis in clusters 1, 3, and 4 indicated significantly lower expression of kidney progenitor markers PAX8, EYA1, CITED1, and HOXB7 in KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: Differential gene expression analysis in these three clusters indicated significantly lower expression of kidney progenitor markers PAX8, EYA1, CITED1, and HOXB7 in KO cells from clusters 1, 3, and 4 when compared to WT cells (Figure 5D, E and F; Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by violin plots in Figure 5D-F and dot plots in Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: scRNA sequencing data showed downregulated expression of genes encoding ciliary proteins, including OFD1, PCM1, and RAB11A in CEP83-deficient cells.
source: Interestingly, scRNA sequencing data also showed downregulated expression of genes encoding ciliary proteins, including OFD1, PCM1, and RAB11A (Ferrante et al., 2006; Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Knödler et al., 2010; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), consistent with the ciliogenesis defects in CEP83 knockout cells.
evidence: This is supported by violin plots in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: A consistent upregulation of genes normally expressed in early LPM, including OSR1, FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2, CXCL12, GATA5, and GATA6, was observed in CEP83−/− cells compared to WT cells at day 7.
source: We next inspected single-cell transcriptomes and bulk RNA sequencing data from D7 cells for genes that were upregulated in CEP83−/− cells compared to WT cells. From this analysis, we observed a consistent upregulation of genes that are normally expressed in early LPM, including OSR1, FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2, CXCL12, GATA5, and GATA6 (Prummel et al., 2020; Mugford et al., 2008b; Mae et al., 2013; Mahlapuu et al., 2001; Ormestad et al., 2004; Wilm et al., 2004; Wotton et al., 2008; Grote et al., 2013; Schindler et al., 2014; Tsuchihashi et al., 2011; McFadden et al., 2005; Firulli et al., 1998; Risebro et al., 2006; Angelo et al., 2000; Perens et al., 2016; Salcedo and Oppenheim, 2003; Liekens et al., 2010; Loh et al., 2016; Koutsourakis et al., 1999; Holtzinger and Evans, 2007; Reiter et al., 1999; Pikkarainen et al., 2004; Laverriere et al., 1994; Zhao et al., 2008; Prummel et al., 2021; Figure 6A–I).
evidence: This is supported by bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data in Figure 6A-I.

claim: CEP83−/− cells entered an aberrant differentiation path assuming a phenotype indicative of broader LPM instead of more specific IM.
source: This suggested that CEP83−/− cells entered an aberrant differentiation path assuming a phenotype indicative of broader LPM instead of more specific IM.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of LPM markers and downregulation of IM markers.

claim: WT cells of clusters 0, 1, 3, and 4 exhibited an IM-like phenotype, while KO cells were shifted toward an LPM-like phenotype.
source: This analysis indicated that WT cells of these clusters exhibited an IM-like phenotype, while KO cells were shifted toward an LPM-like phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by scoring analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The common IM/LPM marker OSR1 was expressed at higher level in KO cells comparing to the WT cells.
source: The common IM/LPM marker OSR1 was expressed at higher level in KO cells comparing to the WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 6A.

claim: The expression of several LPM genes (OSR1, FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2, and CXCL12) was strongly upregulated in KO cells compared to WT cells at day 25.
source: We then inspected RNA-seq data from WT and KO organoids at day 25 for the expression of LPM genes and markers of LPM derivatives. The expression of several LPM genes (OSR1, FOXF1, FOXF2, FENDRR, HAND1, HAND2, and CXCL12) was strongly upregulated in KO cells compared to WT cells suggesting that an LPM-like cell pool persisted in D25 KO organoids (Figure 6A–I).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data in Figure 6A-I.

claim: CEP83−/− organoids showed significant enrichment for expression of orthologs of early LPM genes (p=0.006).
source: Our targeted comparison documented that CEP83−/− organoids showed significant enrichment for expression of orthologs of early LPM genes (p=0.006) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), including OSR1, CXCL12, HAND1/2, KCTD12, PIK3R3, and ZBTB2.
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A subset of LPM genes enriched for expression in CEP83-mutant cells at D25 was indicative of cardiac or cardiopharyngeal (ISL1, TBX1) as well as vascular progenitor (SOX7, SOX11, NAP1L3, LMO2, GATA2) differentiation.
source: A subset of LPM genes enriched for expression in CEP83-mutant cells at D25 of differentiation was indicative of cardiac or cardiopharyngeal (ISL1, TBX1) as well as vascular progenitor (SOX7, SOX11, NAP1L3, LMO2, GATA2) differentiation (Morikawa and Cserjesi, 2004; Cai et al., 2003; Kwon et al., 2009; Laugwitz et al., 2005; Moretti et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2019; Stennard and Harvey, 2005; Baldini, 2005; Chen et al., 2009; Figure 7A–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data in Figure 7A-G.

claim: Three genes of the upregulated LPM genes, namely OSR1, FOXF1, and FOXF2, are downstream genes of hedgehog signaling.
source: Interestingly, three genes of the upregulated LPM genes, namely OSR1, FOXF1, and FOXF2, are downstream genes of hedgehog signaling (Han et al., 2017; Kugler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2017 and Kugler et al., 2015.

claim: HAND2 is upstream of hedgehog signaling.
source: In addition, HAND2 is upstream of hedgehog signaling (Anderson et al., 2012), essential for early embryonic development and regulated by primary cilium (Kugler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2012.

claim: Bulk RNA sequencing data showed significant upregulation of hedgehog signaling components GLI1 and PTCH1 in CEP83−/− cells.
source: Furthermore, bulk RNA sequencing data showed significant upregulation of hedgehog signaling components GLI1 and PTCH1 in CEP83−/− cells (Lee et al., 1997; Villavicencio et al., 2000; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: 11 patients with biallelic mutations of CEP83 have been reported, 8 of which displayed kidney phenotypes.
source: To date, 11 patients with biallelic mutations of CEP83 have been reported, 8 of which displayed kidney phenotypes (Failler et al., 2014; Veldman et al., 2021; Haer-Wigman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Failler et al., 2014; Veldman et al., 2021; Haer-Wigman et al., 2017.

claim: Available kidney histologies from CEP83 mutation patients identified microcystic tubular dilatations, tubular atrophy, thickened basement membranes, and interstitial fibrosis.
source: Available kidney histologies identified microcystic tubular dilatations, tubular atrophy, thickened basement membranes, and interstitial fibrosis.
evidence: This is based on reported clinical data from patients with CEP83 mutations.

claim: Extrarenal phenotypes in CEP83 mutation patients included speech delay, intellectual disability, hydrocephalus, strabismus, retinal degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, hepatic cytolysis, cholestasis, and portal septal fibrosis.
source: Extrarenal phenotypes included speech delay, intellectual disability, hydrocephalus, strabismus, retinal degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, hepatic cytolysis, cholestasis, and portal septal fibrosis with mild thickening of arterial walls and an increase in the number of the biliary canalicules on liver biopsy.
evidence: This is based on reported clinical data from patients with CEP83 mutations.

claim: Among individuals with CEP83 mutations, all but one carried at least one missense mutation or short in-frame deletion, suggesting that CEP83 function may have been partially preserved.
source: Among individuals with CEP83 mutations, all but one carried at least one missense mutation or short in-frame deletion, suggesting that CEP83 function may have been partially preserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the types of mutations reported in patients.

claim: One individual with presumed full loss of CEP83 displayed a more severe phenotype with multiple organ dysfunction.
source: One individual with presumed full loss of CEP83 displayed a more severe phenotype with multiple organ dysfunction.
evidence: This is based on reported clinical data from a patient with CEP83 mutation.

claim: Mice with a targeted homozygous loss-of-function mutation of Cep83 display midembryonic lethality (at E12.5) with evidence of severe developmental delay as early as E9.5.
source: In this regard, it is interesting that mice with a targeted homozygous loss-of-function mutation of their CEP83 ortholog (Cep83tm1.1(KOMP)Vlcg) display midembryonic lethality (at E12.5) with evidence of severe developmental delay as early as E9.5 (https://www.mousephenotype.org/data/genes/MGI:1924298).
evidence: This is based on data from the Mouse Phenotype database.

claim: The primary cilium is critically involved in hedgehog signaling.
source: The primary cilium is critically involved in hedgehog signaling (Ho and Stearns, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho and Stearns, 2021.

claim: Hedgehog signaling is important for mesodermal lineage decisions during gastrulation.
source: Moreover, Hedgehog signaling is important for mesodermal lineage decisions during gastrulation (Guzzetta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guzzetta et al., 2020.

claim: PAX8, EYA1, and HOXB7 are essential for normal kidney development.
source: We observed downregulated expression of the key nephron progenitor genes PAX8, EYA1, and HOXB7 in CEP83−/− cells at day 7, which might explain their failure to differentiate into kidney cells since each of these genes is essential for normal kidney development (Vincent et al., 1997; Pfeffer et al., 1998; Kumar et al., 1998; Bouchard et al., 2002; Xu et al., 1999; Patterson and Potter, 2004; Rojek et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about the role of these genes in kidney development.

claim: Inductive signals from HOXB7-positive ureteric bud are known to maintain viability of nephron progenitor cells in the IM.
source: Furthermore, inductive signals from HOXB7-positive ureteric bud are known to maintain viability of nephron progenitor cells in the IM (Barasch et al., 1997), which may contribute to increased numbers of apoptotic cells we observed in CEP83−/− cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barasch et al., 1997.

claim: In mice, centrosome amplification severely disrupts kidney development, resulting in depletion of renal progenitors and renal hypoplasia.
source: Defects during nephron progenitor differentiation in the IM would be expected to result in severe kidney phenotypes such as renal agenesis or renal hypodysplasia. Defects of centriolar components or cilia have previously been linked to such phenotypes: in mice, centrosome amplification, i.e., the formation of excess centrosomes per cell severely disrupts kidney development, resulting in depletion of renal progenitors and renal hypoplasia (Dionne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dionne et al., 2018.

claim: In humans, loss of KIF14 has been associated with kidney malformations, including renal agenesis and renal dysplasia.

claim: Crosstalk of LPM and IM has been reported previously in zebrafish.
